prompt:
A number $N$ is a two-digit positive integer. It can be written as $\overline{ab}$ to show its digits $a$ and $b$. How can $N$ be written in terms of $a$ and $b$ in standard algebra?

Find all possible $N$ with digits $a$ and $b$, where $N=\overline{ab}$ and $N=a+b^2$.

solutions.title: Digit algebra
solutions.body:
In standard algebra $N=10a+b$ with $1\le a\le9$, $0\le b\le9$.

The condition $10a+b=a+b^2$ gives $9a=b^2-b=b(b-1)$. So $9\mid b(b-1)$. The numbers $b$ and $b-1$ share no prime factor, so $9$ divides one of them (all of the $3$s must go into one factor).

- $9\mid b$: $b=0$ gives $a=0$ (not a two-digit number); $b=9$ gives $9a=72$, $a=8$, $N=89$.
- $9\mid b-1$: $b=1$ gives $a=0$ (not allowed). ($b=10$ is not a digit.)

So the only solution is $N=89$. Check: $8+9^2=89$.

**Answer: $N=10a+b$, and the only possible number is $89$** ∎

prompt:
In the quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AB=AD$ and $AC=DC$. The diagonals of the quadrilateral meet at $E$ and $AE=EB$. Also, $\angle BAC=2\angle BDC$ as shown.

Find the value of $\angle BDC$. Hence prove that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

solutions.title: Chase the angles
solutions.body:
Let $\angle BDC=x^\circ$, so $\angle BAC=2x^\circ$.

- $AE=EB$, so triangle $AEB$ is isosceles with $\angle ABE=\angle BAE=2x^\circ$.
- $AB=AD$, so $\angle ADB=\angle ABD=2x^\circ$ (note $\angle ABD=\angle ABE$).
- Hence $\angle ADC=\angle ADB+\angle BDC=2x+x=3x^\circ$.
- $AC=DC$, so $\angle CAD=\angle CDA=3x^\circ$.

Now the angle at $A$ in triangle $ABD$ is $\angle BAD=\angle BAC+\angle CAD=2x+3x=5x$, so its angle sum gives
$$2x+2x+5x=180,\qquad x=20 .$$
So $\angle BDC=20^\circ$.

**Triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.** Then $\angle CAD=\angle CDA=60^\circ$, so triangle $ACD$ is equilateral and $AC=AD$. Since $AD=AB$, we get $AC=AB$: triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with apex $A$.

**Answer: $\angle BDC=20^\circ$** ∎

prompt:
A cuboid has dimensions $7$ by $8$ by $x$ where $x>8$. A water tank is a cylinder with base area $a$. The cuboid stays at the bottom when water is added.

When the cuboid has the $8$ by $x$ face down, a volume $v$ of water is added to the tank to a depth of $7$, level with the top of the cuboid.

When the cuboid has the $7$ by $x$ face down, the water level drops by $1$.

When the cuboid has the $7$ by $8$ face down, the water level again drops by $1$.

Find how much the water level drops when the cuboid is removed.

solutions.title: Volume of water in each position
solutions.body:
The volume of water is the tank volume up to the water level minus the part occupied by the cuboid.

- $8\times x$ face down: depth $7$, the cuboid fills a cross-section $8x$, so $v=7(a-8x)$.
- $7\times x$ face down: depth $6$, cross-section $7x$, so $v=6(a-7x)$.
- $7\times 8$ face down: depth $5$, cross-section $56$ (and the cuboid is taller than $5$, as $x>8$), so $v=5(a-56)$.

First two: $7a-56x=6a-42x$, so $a=14x$.
Last two: $6a-42x=5a-280$, so $a=42x-280$.
Hence $14x=42x-280$, $x=10$, $a=140$ and $v=7(140-80)=420$.

With no cuboid the depth is $v/a=420/140=3$. The level was $5$, so it drops by $2$ more.

**Answer: 2** ∎

prompt:
A tile is one of the two triangles made by cutting a square of area $3$ in half along the diagonal. In attempting to tile a $49$ by $49$ square floor using these tiles with none of them overlapping and none going outside the square, it is impossible to tile it fully. Find the maximum number of these tiles which can be used in this tiling.

Demonstrate how to do this and prove that no more tiles will fit.

solutions.title: Area bound and a construction
solutions.body:
**Upper bound.** The floor has area $49^2=2401$. Each tile is half of a square of area $3$, so has area $\tfrac32$. Non-overlapping tiles inside the floor satisfy $\tfrac32 T\le 2401$, so $T\le \dfrac{2\cdot2401}{3}=1600.67\ldots$, i.e. $T\le1600$.

**Construction with $1600$ tiles.** The tiles are right isosceles triangles with legs $\sqrt3$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt6$. Put four of them together with their right angles at one point: they form a square of side $\sqrt6$ (area $6$). Arrange $20\times20=400$ such squares in a $20\times20$ grid. This is a square of side $20\sqrt6=\sqrt{2400}<\sqrt{2401}=49$, so it fits inside the floor, and it contains $400\times4=1600$ tiles.

So the maximum is $1600$.

**Answer: 1600** ∎

prompt:
A keypad is a $3$ by $3$ grid with the digits $1$ to $3$ in order on the top row, $4$ to $6$ in order on the second row and $7$ to $9$ in order on the third row.

Seb has the keypad upside-down (i.e. rotated through $180^\circ$) and types his three-digit PIN as if the keypad were the right way up. The number he types in turns out to be $k$ times his original PIN, where $k$ is a positive integer.

Find all possible PINs and prove there are no others.

solutions.title: Each digit $a$ becomes $10-a$
solutions.body:
Rotating the keypad through $180^\circ$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow9$, $2\leftrightarrow8$, $\dots$, so a digit $a$ of the PIN is typed as $10-a$. (No PIN digit is $0$, as there is no $0$ key.)

If the PIN is $x=100a+10b+c$, the typed number is
$$100(10-a)+10(10-b)+(10-c)=1110-x .$$
So $1110-x=kx$, i.e. $(k+1)x=1110=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot37$.

Since $x\ge100$, $k+1=\dfrac{1110}{x}\le11$, and $k+1\ge2$. The divisors of $1110$ in $[2,11]$ are $2,3,5,6,10$, giving
- $k=1$: $x=555$,
- $k=2$: $x=370$, which contains the digit $0$ (no such key), rejected,
- $k=4$: $x=222$,
- $k=5$: $x=185$,
- $k=9$: $x=111$.

Check: $555\to555=1\times555$; $222\to888=4\times222$; $185\to925=5\times185$; $111\to999=9\times111$.

**Answer: $111,\ 185,\ 222,\ 555$** ∎

prompt:
$2025$ penguins ($675$ each of emperors, kings and gentoos) stand in a line from left to right. They may move by performing the *penguin shuffle* in which an emperor takes a king's place, a gentoo takes the position vacated by the emperor and the displaced king takes the place vacated by the gentoo.

Prove that, no matter what the starting order, it is possible to place the emperors on the left, kings in the middle and gentoos on the right after a finite number of shuffles.
answer: First move all gentoos to the right block using single shuffles, then fix the emperor/king blocks by a sequence of three shuffles that swaps a misplaced king and a misplaced emperor and restores everything else (as far as types go).

solutions.title: Two steps
solutions.body:
Only the *types* matter. A shuffle chooses an emperor at position $p$, a king at $q$ and a gentoo at $r$ (anywhere in the line) and changes the types to $p\!:\!G$, $q\!:\!E$, $r\!:\!K$. Call the left $675$ places the E-zone, the middle $675$ the K-zone and the right $675$ the G-zone.

**Step 1: all gentoos into the G-zone.** Suppose some place $t$ in the G-zone does not hold a gentoo. There are $675$ gentoos and fewer than $675$ of them are in the G-zone, so some gentoo $r$ lies outside the G-zone. We increase the number of gentoos in the G-zone without ever removing one from it:
- If $t$ holds an emperor, choose any king $q$ and shuffle $(p,q,r)=(t,q,r)$. Now $t$ holds a gentoo, and the only gentoo that disappeared was $r$, outside the G-zone.
- If $t$ holds a king, choose any emperor $p'$ and shuffle $(p',t,r)$. This puts a gentoo at $p'$ and an emperor at $t$ (and a king at $r$, outside the G-zone). If $p'$ is in the G-zone we have gained a gentoo there. Otherwise $t$ now holds an emperor and, since $p'$ now holds a gentoo outside the G-zone, a gentoo outside the G-zone still exists, so we apply the previous case.

Each round increases the number of gentoos in the G-zone, so after finitely many rounds the whole G-zone is gentoos, and the E-zone and K-zone together hold all $675$ emperors and $675$ kings.

**Step 2: fix the emperors and kings.** Let $u$ be a place in the E-zone holding a king and $w$ a place in the K-zone holding an emperor. Choose another emperor at a place $A$ ($A\ne w$; there are $675\ge2$ emperors) and a gentoo at a place $D$ in the G-zone. Write the types at $(A,u,w,D)$ as $(E,K,E,G)$ and perform three shuffles, each written $(p,q,r)$:
1. $(A,u,D)$: types become $(G,E,E,K)$.
2. $(w,D,A)$: types become $(K,E,G,E)$.
3. $(D,A,w)$: types become $(E,E,K,G)$.

(In each shuffle the three chosen places hold an emperor, a king and a gentoo, as required.) The net effect is $(E,K,E,G)\to(E,E,K,G)$: the king at $u$ and the emperor at $w$ have swapped types, while $A$ and $D$ have the same types as before and nothing else changed.

The E-zone has $675$ places and there are $675$ emperors in the E-zone and K-zone together, so the number of kings in the E-zone equals the number of emperors in the K-zone. Repeating the three-shuffle swap fixes one misplaced pair at a time, and after finitely many repetitions the E-zone holds only emperors and the K-zone only kings, with the G-zone untouched in type.

So the emperors end on the left, kings in the middle and gentoos on the right. ∎
